section_summary: This section documents the immediate political and diplomatic aftermath of the May 15, 1932 Incident in Tokyo, during which Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai was assassinated by cadet and naval conspirators. It records the collapse of party-based government, the consultations of Prince Saionji, and the establishment of a national coalition cabinet headed by Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito under the strong influence of the Army and War Minister Sadao Araki. The file also traces domestic and international tensions, including debates over the recognition of Manchukuo, relations with the League of Nations and the Soviet Union, and diplomatic exchanges of condolence from American missions abroad.

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording a telegram from Shanghai concerning the death of General Yoshinori Shirakawa.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Cunningham's 1932 telegram reporting General Shirakawa's death from Hongkew Park bombing wounds.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding the Death of General Shirakawa

subfiles.about: A telegram reporting on the anticipated foreign, financial, and administrative policies of the incoming Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays a Reuter report that Japan's new cabinet's foreign policy will be more liberal, financial policy moderately inflationist, formally announced at a June 1 Diet session.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 577 from Peiping Transmitting Reuter Report on New Japanese Government Policies

subfiles.about: A despatch reporting the American Ambassador's call of condolence on the Japanese Chargé d'Affaires in Buenos Aires following Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Bliss reports expressing condolences to Buenos Aires's Japanese chargé over Premier Inukai's assassination, enclosing Miyakoshi's grateful acknowledgment confirming the message's relay to Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1638 from Buenos Aires: Assassination of Japanese Prime Minister

subfiles.about: A telegram transmitting a Reuter report of Premier Saito's address to the Diet outlining the administrative policies of the new National Government.
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays Premier Saito's Diet policy speech stressing ending social unrest, relieving agricultural/urban distress, and purifying politics, pledging nonpartisan National Government support from both major parties.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 608 from Peiping Transmitting Reuter Report on Premier Saito's Policy Speech

subfiles.about: A despatch providing a narrative summary of events from May 15 to 19, 1932, surrounding the assassination of Premier Inukai and cabinet negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville provides a detailed chronology of events in Tokyo from May 15 to May 19, 1932, following the fatal shooting of Premier Tsuyoshi Inukai by cadet and naval officers. Simultaneous armed attacks targeted Count Makino, Admiral Suzuki, police headquarters, the Seiyukai party office, and major banks. The report tracks the temporary premiership of Korekiyo Takahashi, internal party debates within the Seiyukai, military demands spearheaded by General Sadao Araki, and the arrival of Prince Saionji in Tokyo to advise the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 623 from Tokyo: Summary of Events - May 15th-19th Connected with the Assassination of Premier Inukai

subfiles.about: A despatch and State Department memorandum analyzing the underlying social, military, and constitutional significance of the May 15 Incident.
subfiles.summary: This subfile consists of a Division of Far Eastern Affairs cover memorandum and Tokyo Despatch No. 624 with enclosed newspaper translations from the Tokyo Asahi and Tokyo Hochi. Neville examines the feudal samurai traditions and public tolerance of patriotic violence that motivated the perpetrators against corrupt party politicians and financial houses. He details connections to the Mito Patriotic School (Aikyojiku) and Blood Brotherhood, outlines the four conditions imposed by the Army for participating in a cabinet as reported in Jiji Shimpo, and discusses constitutional flaws stemming from the erosion of the Genro system.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 624 from Tokyo: Comment on the May 15th Affair, with Department Memorandum and Press Enclosures

subfiles.about: A despatch reviewing German press commentary across the political spectrum regarding the assassination of Premier Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Frederic M. Sackett summarizes German newspaper reactions to the assassination of Premier Inukai, noting unanimous predictions of heightened tension between Japan and Soviet Russia. The report analyzes coverage across right-wing, centrist, and left-wing organs, including the official Korrespondenz, the Nazi Voelkischer Beobachter and Der Angriff, Hugenberg's Lokal-Anzeiger, the Vossische Zeitung, the Social Democratic Vorwaerts, and the Communist Rote Fahne. Commentary linked the events to extreme nationalism, anti-capitalism, and Japan's imperial ambitions in Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1738 from Berlin: Press Reaction to Murder of Japanese Premier

subfiles.about: A special report transmitting and analyzing an article by Dr. A. Legendre in Le Figaro regarding the military and social reaction in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dawson summarizes Dr. Legendre's Le Figaro article arguing Japan's unrest reflects samurai/Ronin reaction against Westernization and rural poverty rather than fascism, emphasizing the army's push for a nonpartisan cabinet against perceived League bias.
subfiles.title: Special Report No. W.D. 1050 from Paris: Dr. Legendre's Opinion on the Japanese Situation

subfiles.about: A despatch forwarding Chinese newspaper editorials discussing the Manchurian situation and the Tokyo assassinations.
subfiles.summary: Minister Nelson T. Johnson transmits three editorials from northern China published after the assassination of Premier Inukai. The Yenching Gazette evaluates Japan's eight months of occupation in Manchuria, noting rampant banditry, heavy costs from the Shanghai war, and rising friction with Russia. Le Journal de Pekin discusses 'Pan-Japanism' and the Tanaka Memorial while citing Karl Radek's warnings in Izvestia, and the Peking & Tientsin Times analyzes the clash between samurai feudal nationalism and modern constitutional governance.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1538 from Peiping: Press Comment on Japanese Political Situation

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and extracted pages from Tokyo Political Report No. 54 detailing the formation of the national Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains a Document File Note (894.00/417) cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 634 (Political Report No. 54) of June 1, 1932, accompanied by pages 12 to 14 of the report. The text describes the political confusion following the May 15 assassinations, the interim leadership of Takahashi, and Prince Saionji's recommendation of Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito as Premier. Neville notes General Araki's retention of the War Ministry, the non-partisan character of the new government, and persistent fears that unrest among younger officers might lead to renewed violence.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 634 (Political Report No. 54) on the Formation of the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: A confidential despatch analyzing the composition, political background, and ministerial personnel of the newly formed Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Preceded by a Document File Note (894.00/418), Tokyo Despatch No. 635 provides a thorough analysis of the coalition cabinet established by Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito. Neville characterizes the administration as a stopgap compromise dominated by War Minister Sadao Araki and the radical young military faction, profiling key ministers including Takahashi (Finance), Yamamoto (Home Affairs), and Okada (Navy). The report details severe domestic and external dilemmas facing the cabinet, including agrarian unrest, corruption, the economic dominance of the Mitsui and Iwasaki (Mitsubishi) families, and the impending League of Nations report on Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 635 from Tokyo: The Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: A telegram surveying the internal and external dilemmas confronting Japan over whether to grant formal recognition to Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Preceded by a Document File Note (894.00/419), Ambassador Joseph C. Grew surveys the major problems confusing the Japanese government regarding the potential recognition of Manchukuo. He details plans for establishing a unified Manchurian administration under military leadership, conflicts over the degree of actual independence for the Changchun regime, and friction between General Honjo and War Minister Araki. The telegram weighs the popular domestic and military clamor for recognition against international complications, including foreign criticism, Nine-Power Treaty violations, customs disputes at Dairen, and heavy financial burdens.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 161 from Tokyo: Survey of Principal Problems Regarding Recognition of Manchukuo

subfiles.about: A despatch transmitting diplomatic correspondence exchanging American condolences on the death of Premier Tsuyoshi Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits condolence notes on Premier Inukai's assassination: Neville's note to Yoshizawa citing his family loss as Inukai's son-in-law, and Yoshizawa's grateful reply.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4 from Tokyo: Expression of Sympathy on the Death of Premier Inukai

subfiles.about: A despatch transmitting press editorials from northern China on the diplomatic implications of the Saito Cabinet and proposed conferences.
subfiles.summary: Perkins forwards editorials on whether the Saito Cabinet improves Sino-Japanese settlement prospects, questioning whether either government is stable enough to negotiate and enforce a Manchuria compromise after Japan's Shanghai withdrawal.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1564 from Peiping: Press Comment on the Political Situation in Japan and the Saito Cabinet
